These books are designed for beginners and teach the basics of many popular modern dishes, not just from pre-sliced cuts, but the actual butchery and preparation involved, turning you from a humble cook to an excellent chef, one that never needs a recipe, just to know what's available and how many people are being served.

With this in mind let's begin.

  • Cook with Jamie - Jamie Oliver. Excellent beginners resource with many crowd pleasing modern recipes and skills in a nice design hardcover. An international taste compendium, hard to find something you won't love. Probably his best work in my opinion, healthy and delicious recipes.

  • The Professional Chef - American Culinary Institute. An excellent, thick hardcover that is beautifully set out. Almost every kind of 4/5 star restaurant recipe basic, and a few twists to get you started. The book includes great diagrams, technique explanations and its biggest asset is its sheer volume of ingredient preparation recipes. E.g. steaming times for the different kinds of cabbages, best techniques for different varieties of potatoes. Also for you guys in US I'm pretty sure it has season periods and a whole load of info.

  • Leith's Meat Bible - Max Clark & Susan Spall. Make your meat meals a lot cheaper by buying larger cuts and portioning yourself for the week. Also, the larger cuts will generally be fresher and not be coated with carbon monoxide. We can get to whole animals and more interesting parts later! The book includes great diagrams, technique reasoning explanations and the basics for all kinds of foods, which you can customise flavours, sweetness, etc after you master.

  • The Silver Spoon - Celia Donfrio or something... The book is basically the Italian version of the American Culinary Institute, but much older and not updated very much, but the recipes in there are fantastic if you want to experience true Italian cuisine with recipes from scratch.

  • Larousse Gastronmique - Prosper Montagne, an even older book dating from pre-WW2. Same as The Silver Spoon but for French cuisine. Get the latest editions though, as they are almost on par with The Professional Chef as far as their diagrams and techniques, which of course are still delicious.

Now, you might think there is a lot of crossover material if you go out and buy them all at once (not recommended, too much info and wasted capital, master them in order of the first three, then your choice of next cuisine.

Personally, I recommend French as if you live in one of your U.S food deser areas it is easier to cover up lessor ingredients with great sauces, whereas Italian cuisine relies on ingredient selection, freshness and quality.

As a rule for cuisine recipe searches, you can generally rely that the colder the climate, the more heavy the dish calorie wise and more sauce based seasoning or thicker starch based soup, the hotter the environment, the lighter the dish, spicier and more dressing/dip/paste based seasoning or thin broth based soup.

Supplementary for experienced home cooks:

  • Charcuterie - Michael Ruhlman & BrianPoleyn. Name says it all, pretty much everything you need to know about preserving your precious proteins such as home made corned beef, prosciutto to my favourite and king of all charcuterie, Guanciale. Great resource for learning what to do with every part of the animal, beyond fresh recipes. Decent diagrams, but not a photo book.

And finally for men:

  • Seven Fires - Francis Mallman. This book has a South American focus on preparing meats on a much larger scale, all kinds of wood fire, pizza oven and very hot, very heavy recipes and techniques. Men, unless you know things like how to rig up a home spit with a foot turning pedal with some rope, soaked wood and metal, you have skills that you need to learn, that may one day be very useful in our lifetimes.

You don't want your partner tired and covered in soot and wood smoke either. Much nicer to come grab her, make her dirty (make sure she isn't doing anything time sensitive!), good excuse for a mid cook out break and shower.
